chunks: Thermal relief pads and rework difficulty. The question: Often times many power components or ground components have thermal relief pads. How does this impact reworkability?
A pad that is joined solidly to a big copper plane is hard to desolder, because the plane carries the heat away as fast as your tool delivers it.
A thermal relief joins the pad to the plane through a few thin spokes, so less heat drains away and the solder melts more easily.
Thin spokes carry less current, so power pads often stay solid.
Imagine filling a bucket with a big hole in the side up to a marked line. Water level stands for temperature, and the marked line is the solder's melting point.
A big hole (a plane) means you must pour very fast. A thermal relief shrinks the hole. Preheating the board is like filling the bucket partway before you start.
Tool power flows into the joint node and out through two thermal resistances in series to the board temperature. The joint temperature rise is P times (R relief plus R spread) .
Removing the relief removes R relief (and shrinks the spread resistance because the pad touches the plane at a smaller radius), so the same power produces a smaller rise.
Copper plane: a large sheet of copper in the board, usually for power or ground. Thermal relief: a pad joined to a plane by thin spokes.
Melting point of solder: the temperature where it turns fully liquid, about 217 degrees Celsius for common lead-free solder.
Thermal resistance: how many degrees hotter the joint stays than the board for each watt of heat you push in, in K/W (a kelvin step equals a degree Celsius).
Preheat: warming the whole board first, so the tool has less temperature to add.
Say a solid pad has a thermal resistance of about 41. 4 K/W to the rest of the board. From 25 degrees Celsius you need 192 degrees more to reach 217 degrees Celsius.
That takes 192 ÷ 41. 4 about 4. 6 watts. Add a relief and the resistance rises to about 58 K/W, so you need only about 3. 3 watts.
Preheat to 120 degrees Celsius and the step is only 97 degrees, so the solid pad needs about 2. 3 watts. It is a rough model: trust the trends, not the exact watts.
That is the whole idea.

"Thermal reliefs make rework easier because a pad tied solidly to a plane sits on a heat sink; the plane carries away the heat from the iron or nozzle, so the joint struggles to reach solder liquidus.
Spokes limit that heat flow. But power and ground pads often need the low-resistance connection, so reliefs get omitted there and those joints become the hardest to rework.
I'd compensate with bottom preheat, a bigger tip or hot air, and flux."
